title: Chronic unpredictable stress induces negative cognitive bias in rats with sex-specific changes in neurogenesis and functional connectivity
authors: Namchuk, A. B.; Hodges, T.; McGovern, A.; Galea, L.
abstract: Background: Females are more likely to be diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD) than males. Cognitive symptoms of MDD include negative cognitive bias, the perception of ambiguous situations as negative, which predicts MDD episode onset and severity. MDD is associated with changes to functional connectivity between regions involved in cognition, emotion, attention, and memory. Methods: Here we examined the impact of chronic unpredictable stress (CUS) on negative cognitive bias in male (n=18) and female (n=22) Sprague-Dawley rats. We assessed hippocampal neurogenesis and c-Fos expression in response to an ambiguous context across 15 regions of the frontal cortex, amygdala, nucleus accumbens, and hippocampus, including in newborn dentate gyrus (DG) neurons, to examine functional connectivity during cognitive bias testing. We conducted a graph-based network analysis and constructed linear models to predict freezing in the ambiguous context based on regional activation. Results: CUS-exposed rats froze more to the ambiguous context than non-CUS-exposed rats, regardless of sex. CUS decreased neurogenesis in the ventral DG of both sexes, and increased activation of new neurons in the dorsal DG of males only. In response to the ambiguous context, CUS males had an increase in c-Fos expression in the amygdala. CUS produced extensive, sex-specific network reorganization, decreasing global network efficiency in males but not in females. Freezing in the ambiguous context was predicted by activation of new neurons in combination with the ventral CA1 in opposing directions across sex. Conclusions: These findings suggest that sex-specific pathways drive the expression of CUS-induced negative cognitive bias, underscoring the necessity of sex-stratified preclinical and clinical research on negative cognitive bias in depression.

title: MRI-free OPM-MEG recovers medial temporal lobe theta during scene imagination
authors: Thornberry, C.; Math, P.; Cohen Serra, M.; Seymour, R.; Nolan, C.; Whelan, R.
abstract: Optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) offers a wearable, movement-tolerant alternative to conventional cryogenic MEG, placing sensors closer to the scalp and, in principle, improving sensitivity to deep sources. This is advantageous for examining subcortical structures that are affected by ageing, disorders and disease, such as the hippocampus. However, it remains unclear whether well-established activity (such as the attenuation of theta oscillations during the imagination of novel scenes) can be recovered from the medial temporal lobe (MTL) with OPM-MEG, and whether an individual structural MRI is required. Here, fifteen adults completed a scene imagination task. Initially we applied a 12-parameter template warping coregistration pipeline to the full sample. Following source reconstruction, we recovered the expected attenuation of theta (4-8 Hz) power during scene imagination compared to a counting baseline, with a significant cluster of activity peaking in the left parahippocampal gyrus. The clusters centre of mass was localised to the left hippocampus (t = -3.55, p = 0.048, whole-brain FWE-corrected) and was mostly confined to the left medial temporal lobe. We further supported our findings by using an individual T1-weighted MRI reconstruction pipeline in six participants who had these scans available. The two approaches produced similar whole-brain topographies and localised the peak MTL theta effect to left hippocampus, with temporal-lobe conjunction centroids 3-mm apart. These findings provide evidence that the theta attenuation of the scene construction network can be recovered at the group level with OPM-MEG, without an individual MRI.

title: Conserved Laminar-Cellular Architecture Predicts the Spectrolaminar Motif
authors: Mulvey, A. G.; Lichtenfeld, M. J.; Nejat, H.; Xiong, Y. S.; Carlson, B. M.; Mitchell, B. A.; Mendoza-Halliday, D.; Westerberg, J. A.; Maier, A.; Duque, A.; Bastos, A. M.
abstract: We recently identified the spectrolaminar motif, a layer-resolved pattern of local field potential (LFP) power, which is preserved across many areas of the primate cortex. It remains unclear which specific cytoarchitectonic features can explain the spectrolaminar motif. To investigate this, we performed histological and neurophysiological analyses of 11 brain areas spanning the macaque cortical hierarchy to examine the relationship between the laminar patterns of LFP power and the laminar distributions of cellular density for parvalbumin, calbindin, and calretinin interneurons, and pyramidal neurons. We tested whether cellular distributions are conserved and if they predict the corresponding variation in LFP power comprising the spectrolaminar motif. We found that the cytoarchitectonic and spectrolaminar data were intrinsically low-dimensional, with two-component patterns conserved across areas, and that the spectrolaminar motif could be predicted from these laminar cellular gradients. Critically, the regression coefficients mapping structure (cytoarchitecture) to function (spectrolaminar motif) were themselves highly conserved across areas, suggesting that a common cellular-to-spectral rule operates throughout cortex rather than a distinct rule per region. To evaluate this structure-function model, we tested it against post-mortem data from schizophrenia patients. We tested whether empirically-observed cytoarchitectonic changes from postmortem studies on inhibitory interneuron dysfunction in schizophrenia could be used to predict spectrolaminar alterations using our structure-function model. We found that they did, and that the functional changes match what is known from non-invasive neurophysiology in schizophrenia. This work moves beyond simple structure-function correlation to establish a predictive mathematical framework that informs healthy and aberrant brain circuitry.

title: Fixel-wise Differences in White Matter Fiber-bundle Cross-section identified in Children who Stutter
authors: Weerathunge, H.; Liu, Y.; Hobler, F.; Angstadt, M.; Jahn, A.; Chow, H. M.; Chang, S.-E.
abstract: Developmental stuttering has been repeatedly linked to decreased white matter integrity and structural connectivity differences in major white matter tracts. Prior diffusion-weighted MRI studies reporting such white matter structural differences involved voxel-averaged tensor measures (e.g., fractional anisotropy (FA)). A well-acknowledged limitation of this approach, however, has been that it cannot resolve distinct fiber populations within crossing-fiber regions. Fixel-based analysis addresses this limitation by quantifying individual fiber populations within a voxel and providing complementary measures of fiber density (FD), fiber-bundle cross-section (FC), and their combined measure (FDC).Here we applied Fixel-based analysis to diffusion MRI data from 171 children aged 3 - 13 years, including 84 children who stutter and 87 typically developing controls, to test whether white-matter differences associated with developmental stuttering were expressed as differences in FD, FC, and FDC and whether these measures show group-specific age-related patterns. We evaluated this at both the whole-brain level and within a priori white-matter tracts.FC, but not FD or FDC, showed significant Group and Group by Age effects, indicating that white-matter differences were primarily expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure. Tract-of-interest analyses identified developmental differences in bilateral arcuate fasciculus FC that remained significant across tracts, with controls showing greater age-related increases in FC than children who stutter. Additional FC differences were observed across corticospinal and thalamocortical pathways, although these tract-wise effects were less robust to across-tract correction. These findings suggest that white-matter differences in developmental stuttering are prominently expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure rather than fiber density and highlight divergent development of bilateral arcuate pathways. FBA provides fiber-specific information that complements conventional tensor-based diffusion measures and may improve characterization of white-matter development in childhood stuttering.

title: Desmin Mutations Disrupt Filament Elongation and Drive Polymorphic Aggregation
authors: Schween, L.; Burchert, J.-P.; van der Heyden, M.; Schultheis, D.; Muecke, N.; Koester, S.; Strelkov, S. H.; Herrmann, H.; Fabry, B.
abstract: In muscle cells, desmin intermediate filaments form a cytoskeletal network that maintains the structural integrity and mechanical coupling of myofibrils. Dominant missense mutations in desmin cause myopathies characterized by intracellular protein aggregation. To explore the process of aggregate formation, we investigate the assembly kinetics of wild-type desmin and four disease-associated variants (N342D, L345P, R350P, and R406W) using dual-wavelength stopped-flow spectroscopy, complemented by atomic force microscopy and molecular dynamics simulations. At low ionic strength, all proteins form uniform tetramers. Increasing the ionic strength initiates assembly by rapid lateral association of tetramers into unit-length filaments (ULFs), followed by longitudinal elongation and radial filament compaction. R406W forms ULFs with wild-type-like kinetics, whereas N342D, L345P, and R350P exhibit delayed lateral assembly. After short filaments have formed, all four mutants diverge from productive filament maturation, but through distinct pathways. Quantitative analysis of atomic force microscopy images together with kinetic modelling of the spectroscopic data shows that wild-type filaments elongate continuously, whereas R406W filaments progressively associate into fibrillar clusters and cease elongating. By contrast, N342D, L345P, and R350P rapidly collapse into globular complexes that subsequently coalesce into larger aggregates. Molecular dynamics simulations indicate that the mutations differentially destabilize coil 2, which leads to local structural perturbations and mutation-specific assembly defects. Together, these findings identify early filament maturation - when elongating ULF-derived filaments would normally undergo radial compaction to form stable, mature filaments - as a critical time point in desmin assembly. At this stage, pathogenic mutations redirect the internal reorganization of the filament from productive stabilization toward mutation-specific structural collapse and aggregation.

title: Tetradic Dynamics of Dyadic Sensorimotor Coordination: A Multiscale EEG Hyperscanning Study
authors: Olarewaju, E.; Palaniyappan, L.; Dumas, G.
abstract: How do leader and follower roles shape the brain mechanisms that support coordinated action between people? This question has therapeutic relevance for conditions such as schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder, where the capacity for reciprocal social coordination is a defining vulnerability. Here, we propose a tetradic framework and examine sensorimotor coordination in 16 healthy adult pairs (15 included in EEG analyses) using dual-brain EEG hyperscanning and a 2x2 within-subject design crossing Role (Leader/Follower) and Condition (Mirroring/Matching). Mirroring required resonance with a partner's movement; Matching required its controlled transformation. This contrast was designed to dissociate automatic from controlled coordination. Behaviourally, Mirroring produced a robust Follower reaction-time advantage: pooling an independent behavioural-only cohort (combined N=64) revealed a smaller Leader advantage, consistent with role-dependent attention-inhibition gating. At the neural level, tonic power and significant phasic condition clusters were greater during Matching than Mirroring, while role-dependent phasic clusters suggested an anticipatory sequence around Leader responses and post-response gating and rebound around Follower responses. Information-theoretic decomposition identified Leader-unique predictive information in superior temporal regions and a separate frontal-pole interaction, Follower-unique predictive information in insular and superior frontal regions, sparse Synergy in the right rostral anterior cingulate cortex, and Redundancy spanning multiple cortical regions. These findings characterize tetradic coordination within dyads as a multiscale, role-asymmetric architecture in which top-down predictive control and bottom-up adaptive regulation are functionally dissociable. The tetradic framework provides a scaffold for this dissociation, and the role-specific signatures it reveals may offer candidate biomarkers for clinical populations in whom interpersonal coordination is disrupted.

title: Predictable Timing Enhances the Use of Predictable Content
authors: Magnusson, O.; Hobbelen, H.; Berkhof, W.; Sack, A. T.; Leunissen, I.; ten Oever, S.
abstract: As events unfold, they carry structure in both their timing and content, with these dimensions often interrelated. Most research has treated these dimensions separately, although processing them jointly may provide important computational benefits. It is an open question whether the brain processes a sequence's timing and predictable content structure independently, or integrates these two sources of information to guide prediction. We hypothesised that predictable timing would allow listeners to better exploit structure in the content, with this effect increasing as content structure becomes stronger. To test this, we presented tone sequences with pitch trajectories following a 1/f^{beta} structure, where {beta} determines how strongly the content of each tone persists, while independently varying the temporal periodicity of the sequence. Performance was quantified using response errors relative to outcome predictions of a Gaussian Process Regression model and a model-free measure of how strongly preceding tones influenced responses. Response error decreased and reliance on preceding tones increased with higher {beta} and periodic timing. Moreover, the influence of preceding tones showed an interaction between timing and content, such that the effect of periodicity grew with increasing {beta}. The response error showed no such interaction, although the effect of periodic timing was reliable only for the most structured sequences. Our findings suggest an interdependency between content and timing, where predictable timing helps listeners make greater use of predictable content.

title: Auditory-motor interactions are sensitive to adaptation and learning on multiple timescales
authors: Zhang, H.; Cantisani, G.; Shamma, S.
abstract: Auditory-motor learning is critical for mastering the production of complex sounds, such as speaking and playing music. It is anchored upon internal models of interactions between actions and their sensory consequences, which are fine-tuned by minimizing the errors between the predicted and received sound. Here, we investigated the neural dynamics of sensorimotor learning by manipulating sensorimotor surprisal, with high surprisal defined as unexpected changes in the mapping between actions and their auditory outcomes. Participants performed a piano-playing task in which the key-to-pitch mapping switched unpredictably among three configurations, creating a dynamic sensorimotor environment that required ongoing adaptation. At the change boundaries, a signature of violated motor-to-auditory predictions was found in the auditory evoked responses at N100, which could not be attributed to either purely auditory surprisals or motor execution errors. This prediction error is modulated by short-term context, with greater error responses following longer periods of no map change, indicating that the brain continuously tracks short-term map contexts and rapidly adapts to them. In contrast, 30 minutes of extended goal-directed training on a single key-pitch map modulated P50 amplitude only for the trained map, a modulation that can be explained by a slow, training-driven update of the sensorimotor map. Hence, while auditory predictions from motor actions can be implicitly learned within short-term contexts for rapid adaptation, the complementary process of building a reliable sensorimotor map requires targeted training sustained over time. Our approach of studying auditory-motor surprisal in time-varying sequences reveals that auditory-motor learning is fast, context-sensitive, and shaped by both short- and long-term experience.

title: A multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with repeated experience sampling
authors: Shareef-Trudeau, L.; Braun, D.; Bounyarith, T.; Li, J.; Peng, H.; Kucyi, A.
abstract: The integration of electroencephalography (EEG) and functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) can be used to characterize temporal and spatial components of neural activity during unfolding mental experience. Here we introduce a multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with measures of continuous behavior and spontaneous mental experience. Data components, organized in Brain Imaging Dataset Structure (BIDS) format, include fMRI, EEG with carbon wire loop sensors for artifact removal, continuous performance task responses, experience sampling ratings, and mental health surveys, from 24 healthy adults. Tasks included the gradual-onset continuous performance task and resting state with intermittent experience sampling of 13 unique thought dimensions (36 repetitions, including 468 total ratings, per participant). The same protocol was completed on two different days, yielding approximately 1.33 hours of simultaneous EEG-fMRI data per individual. The dataset may be used to explore the behavioral and experiential relevance of brain activity during the wakeful resting state. The dataset also provides a means to study the reliability of relationships between fMRI and EEG features across sessions within individuals.

title: Sequential Sampling as a Computational Principle of Episodic Memory
authors: Kerren, C.; Dixit, S.; Coxon, E.; Nikolaev, A. R.; Doeller, C. F.
abstract: Visual perception unfolds through sequential eye movements, yet computational models of episodic memory typically assume that event representations already exist. Here, we propose that sequential gaze sampling does not simply supply memory with visual information, but helps construct the representations that are subsequently stored and retrieved. We introduce a computational model in which successive fixation-dependent samples are integrated into an evolving internal representation before one-shot storage in associative memory. Within individual elements, successive samples progressively individuate the representation; across elements, transitions promote relational integration. Crucially, both effects arise from the same history-dependent updating process where each new sample is integrated into a state already shaped by what came before. As a result, sampling history becomes embedded in the memory representation itself. Changing the order of otherwise identical samples alters both the resulting representation and element-specific retrieval, while reinstating the original sampling trajectory facilitates access to the stored memory. Model-neural analysis further show that changes in the model's evolving representations correspond to neural representational dynamics in lateral temporal cortex. Together, these findings support sequential sampling as a candidate computational process for constructing representations available to episodic memory, linking ongoing perceptual sampling to subsequent memory formation and retrieval.

title: Multimodal profiling and intersectional genetics reveal CA1 border inhibitory neuron diversity and postnatal emergence of retrosplenial connectivity
authors: Martinez Vizcaino, N.; Thrupp, N.; Lorente-Echeverria, B.; Daaboul, D.; Alabi, M.; Milian Alastruey, C.; Linaro, D.; Fourne, Y.; Vandenbempt, J.; Lukacsovich, D.; Földy, C.; Lamote, J.; Wojno, M.; Poovathingal, S.; Fiers, M.; Wierda, K.; Lim, L.; Calafate, S.; De Wit, J.
abstract: Inhibitory neurons (INs) at the stratum radiatum/stratum lacunosum-moleculare border of hippocampal CA1 comprise diverse populations, including long-range-projecting neurons that innervate the retrosplenial cortex (RSCtx). However, their molecular organization and developmental connectivity remain poorly understood. Here, we combine multimodal transcriptomic profiling, intersectional genetics, and retrograde tracing to characterize CA1 border INs. We identified two major caudal ganglionic eminence-derived, Cxcl14-enriched populations distinguished by Syt6/Cck-related and Ntng1-expressing transcriptional profiles. We then generated a Cxcl14-Cre mouse line that, when combined with an IN-specific viral enhancer, provides genetic access to CA1 border INs. Retrograde labeling established that CA1 INs projecting to the RSCtx belong to the Ntng1-expressing population, and that this long-range projection emerges during postnatal mouse development, between postnatal days 3 and 5. Finally, analysis of genes encoding cell-surface proteins, key regulators of connectivity, revealed distinct expression profiles in RSCtx-projecting and SYT6-positive INs. Together, these findings establish a molecular and developmental framework for CA1 border IN diversity and provide a genetic strategy for investigating the assembly and function of these inhibitory circuits.

title: Structural plasticity and enhanced fear extinction following psilocybin in chronically stressed mice
authors: Knox, C. A.; Woodburn, S. C.; Gilbert, A. D.; Schlotzhauer, J. M.; Kwan, A. C.
abstract: The classic psychedelic psilocybin elicits long-lasting neural plasticity and behavioral effects, but prior studies largely examined stress-naive animals. Using longitudinal imaging, we show that psilocybin increases dendritic spine density in frontal cortical neurons and facilitates fear extinction after chronic restraint stress, demonstrating psilocybin's effects in a translationally relevant mouse model.

title: Molecular features underlying functional and structural interactions between diverse transcription regulatory elements in a chromosomal context
authors: Jin, Y.; Hasegawa, Y.; Zhou, Z.; Lin, J. Q.; Leung, A. K.-Y.; Yu, H.; Lis, J.
abstract: Transcription is modulated by interactions among transcription regulatory elements (TREs), including promoters and enhancers, but their underlying interaction specificities remain opaque. Here, we develop a Chromatin-Integrated, landing-pad-based Enhancer Reporter Assay, CIERA-seq, that interrogates regulatory interactions between target promoters and distal TREs (dTREs) in a controlled genomic and chromatin context. We found both promoter-derived (pdTREs) and enhancer-derived-dTREs (edTREs) exhibit enhancer activities on target promoters with a specificity that depends on factors that dTREs recruit. pdTREs are generally enriched for factors involved in the core transcription process, whereas edTREs are enriched for pioneer factors, SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers, and histone acetyltransferase EP300. To further leverage the chromatin integration system, we applied deaminase-based footprinting to profile chromatin accessibility across individual fibers containing distinct target promoter-dTRE pairs. We found that different target promoters and dTREs exhibited distinct accessibility profiles, and that dTREs could modulate the accessibility of their cognate target promoters in a transcription factor and cofactor-dependent manner. Moreover, promoter accessibility was positively associated with transcriptional activity, linking dTRE-mediated changes in local chromatin accessibility to functional transcriptional output. Overall, our CIERA-seq assays and deamination-based footprinting assays support a model where dTREs activate target promoters constrained at different rate limiting steps in transcription by supplying complementary components of the transcription regulatory machinery.

title: Comprehensive protease specificity profiling
authors: Zhu, B.; Lane, M. D.; Baller, J. A.; Jagtap, P. D.; Griffin, T. J.; Seelig, B.
abstract: Protease enzymes are of great importance in medicine, industry, and as research tools. Despite the crucial need for detailed knowledge of their proteolytic cleavage specificity, many proteases are poorly characterized. We present a method for fully characterizing the cleavage specificity of proteases through the comprehensive profiling of all possible permutations of octamer peptide substrates in a single experiment. The powerful combination of in vitro selection with high-throughput sequencing, mass spectrometry, and automated motif mining enabled the screening of mixtures of around 1012 peptides. We developed freely available software that easily integrates the massive amounts of cleavage data into user-friendly specificity information. We applied this method to three different proteases that had either hard-to-study broad specificity (ADAM17 and streptopain) or narrow specificity (factor Xa) as a control. The resulting specificity maps revealed motifs that corroborate canonical known cleavage sites, yet step further into extended spectrum preferences and yield insights into the function of broad specificity proteases.

title: DCAF: Unifying Data Validity, Evaluation Validity and Predictive Modeling for Single-cell Perturbation Simulation
authors: Xia, T.; Lei, C.; Chen, N.; Hou, H.; Gong, C.; Zhang, H.; Qin, H.; Hu, L.; Wang, D.; Li, Q.; Zhang, Y.; Fang, S.; Li, Y.
abstract: Single-cell perturbation profiling is limited by cost and throughput, while computational methods remain constrained by inconsistent evaluation and underperformance relative to simple baselines. Here we present DCAF, a unified framework for single-cell perturbation simulation that that jointly addresses data validity, evaluation validity and predictive modeling. Among its three components, DCAF-data addresses the single-measurement limitation by reconstructing pre- and post-perturbation status using entropy-regularized optimal transport, and is demonstrated on both cell line and multi-cell type datasets. DCAF-criterion evaluates log fold changes in non-silenced genes to improve sensitivity to model error and robustness to zero inflation noise, validated on synthetic datasets. DCAF-model combines JEPA with explicit modeling for regulatory-dynamics modeling for interpretable prediction. Across benchmarks, DCAF outperforms state-of-the-art deep-learning methods, as well as mean and linear baselines in cross-gene, cross-cell-type and cross-region generalization. In adult Mouse brain, DCAF recapitulates known cell-type-specific regulatory heterogeneity of Dgcr8 knockdown at both cell type and gene levels. DCAF thus provides a rigorous and biologically grounded foundation for reliable perturbation simulation across development, disease and therapeutic discovery.

title: Hippocampal-somatomotor coactivation and perceived benefit following Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Life in healthcare students: An exploratory randomized study
authors: Clairis, N.; Saccaro, L. F.; Delplanque, S.; Holman, C.; Celen, Z.; Cachet, C.; Serquet, C.; Meuleman, B.; Bondolfi, G.; Jermann, F.; Rudaz, S.; Piguet, C.
abstract: Mindfulness-based interventions are known to enhance emotion regulation and stress management, yet their neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Effective coping strategies for emotion regulation and stress management would be particularly beneficial for healthcare students, frequently exposed to highly stressful situations. Based on prior work implicating hippocampal-somatomotor dynamics in emotion regulation, we tested whether Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Life (MBCT-L) modulates hippocampal micro-coactivation patterns (CAPs) in healthcare students. In a randomized controlled study including 161 healthcare students, 57 participants (39 females; mean age: 23+/-5 years old) completed resting-state fMRI before and after the 8-weeks intervention and were allocated to MBCT-L (N = 24) or a no-intervention control (N = 33) condition. Hippocampus-seeded CAPs analysis identified six recurrent patterns, including a somatomotor network. MBCT-L improved self-reported mindfulness, but no significant Group*Time interaction for hippocampus-somatomotor coactivation or resting physiological measures was found. In the MBCT-L group, higher hippocampus-somatomotor co-activity was associated with higher perceived importance of the intervention, perceived long-lasting benefits, and post-intervention mindfulness scores. This study suggests that the capacity to up-regulate hippocampus-somatomotor coactivation may index part of the individual benefit derived from mindfulness, supporting its role as a tool for emotion regulation and stress management.

title: Genomic deletion and duplication effects on cognitive ability lie at the opposing ends of the cortical sensorimotor-association hierarchy
authors: Kumar, K.; Kazem, S.; Yang, J.; Benitiere, F.; Diop, M. S.; Clark, B.; Huguet, G.; Engchuan, W.; Kopal, J.; Renne, T.; Shanta, O.; Thiruvahindrapuram, B.; MacDonald, J. R.; Mollon, J.; Schultz, L. M.; Knowles, E. E. M.; Porteous, D.; Davies, G.; Redmond, P.; Harris, S. E.; Cox, S. R.; Schumann, G.; Pausova, Z.; Greenwood, C. M. T.; Paus, T.; Scherer, S. W.; Almasy, L.; Sebat, J.; Glahn, D.; Dumas, G.; Jacquemont, S.
abstract: Cognitive deficits are common across many neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions, including those studied in the current set of PGC-CNV papers. How changes in regional gene expression across the cerebral cortex influence cognitive ability remains unknown. Population variation in gene dosage, which significantly impacts gene expression, represents a unique paradigm to address this question. We developed a cerebral-cortex gene-set burden analysis (CC-GSBA) to associate a trait with genomic deletions and duplications that disrupt genes with similar expression profiles across 180 cortical regions. We performed CC-GSBA across 180 cortical regions to test associations with cognitive ability in 258,292 individuals from general population cohorts. Most cortical gene sets were associated with a decrease in cognitive ability when deleted or duplicated, and this approach revealed opposing cortical patterns for the effect sizes of deletions and duplications. These cortical patterns of effect sizes followed the cortical hierarchy previously characterized at the molecular, cellular, and functional levels. We show that genes with preferential expression in sensorimotor regions demonstrated the largest effect on cognition when deleted. At the opposing end of the cortical hierarchy, genes with preferential expression in multimodal association regions affected cognition the most when duplicated. This cortical pattern of gene dosage response could not be explained by particular cell types, developmental epochs, or genetic constraints, highlighting the fact that the macroscopic network organization of the cerebral cortex is key to understanding the effects of gene dosage on cognitive traits.

title: Modular functional brain network organization contributes to training-related changes in task switching in children
authors: Schwarze, S. A.; Lindenberger, U.; Bunge, S.; Fandakova, Y.
abstract: Cognitive training often aims to improve cognitive skills, but improvements in cognitive performance have been variable. One factor that has been found to predict training outcomes is the degree of modularity of functional brain networks, defined as the extent to which brain regions are more strongly connected to regions within the same functional subnetwork than to regions outside of the subnetwork. Specifically, more modular organization of functional brain networks at baseline has been associated with greater benefits from cognitive training in adults. During childhood, cognitive development is marked by a slow progression towards network integration and segregation, which together contribute to increasing modularity. Thus, network modularity might also be an important predictor of training outcomes in children. To investigate whether individual differences in network modularity predict outcomes of task-switching training in children, we examined 87 children aged 8 to 11 years who completed nine weeks of varying amounts of task-switching training. Prior to training, children showed lower network modularity than adults, in line with previously reported developmental changes in network configuration. More modular organization of functional brain networks before training was associated with higher overall accuracy during task switching and with faster improvements in integrated speed-accuracy scores, especially at the beginning of training. These results suggest that more modular functional networks might allow for faster adaptation to training demands in children and thus faster improvements with training.

title: Polyaxonal A1 amacrine cells form a spatially extended network in primate retina
authors: Boniec, S. L.; Rieke, F.; Manookin, M.
abstract: Inhibitory networks shape information processing in the brain by integrating signals across space, regulating neuronal responses, and controlling the flow of signals through neural circuits. Understanding these computations requires linking the structure of individual inhibitory neuron types to their functional properties and network connectivity. The retina provides a tractable system for meeting this challenge, yet the organization of many retinal inhibitory circuits remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a population of polyaxonal amacrine cells recorded using multielectrode arrays as A1 amacrine cells, a morphologically defined interneuron type in primate retina. This identification is supported by a correspondence between properties of morphologically-identified A1 cells from single cell recordings and putative A1 amacrines in the array recordings. We then identified recursive bistratified ganglion cells in the array recordings based on their electrical coupling to A1 cells, linking this inhibitory network to retinal output pathways. A1 and recursive bistratified cells also share an asymmetry in receptive-field organization, with larger On than Off centers. Finally, A1 spike amplitudes decline during bursts, and analyses of their electrical images suggest that this change may cause some spikes to fail to propagate through their extensive axonal arbors. These findings establish the cellular identity and network organization of a long-range inhibitory circuit in the primate retina and reveal how neuronal architecture, connectivity, and spike dynamics may jointly shape the transmission of visual information.

title: Effects of bromodomain protein inhibition in a mouse model of Niemann-Pick type C disease
authors: Parente, M.; Barthelemy, A.; Caputo, S.; Charlery-Adele, N.; Galmiche, C.; Tonini, C.; Lobasso, S.; Prtvar, D.; Tahirovic, S. W.; Reibel, S.; Pfrieger, F. W.; Pallottini, V.
abstract: Defects in lysosomal lipid handling provoke fatal disorders presenting neurovisceral symptoms with variable onset and life spans. A prime example is Niemann-Pick type C disease (NPCD), where export of cholesterol and other lipids from the endosomal-lysosomal system is impaired due to variants of either NPC intracellular cholesterol transporter 1 (NPC1) or NPC intracellular cholesterol transporter 2 (NPC2). Therapeutic options for NPCD are limited to palliative care and disease-modifying drugs, and there is an unmet need for new treatments. Based on positive effects in patient-derived fibroblasts in vitro, we explored here how inhibition of bromodomain and extra-terminal domain (BET) proteins, a family of histone acetylation readers, affects a well-established mouse model bearing the frequent I1061T variant of NPC1. To this end, we used employed intraperitoneal administration of the blood-brain-barrier penetrating drug JQ1 or vehicle (dimethylsulfoxide), and gauged drug effects based on weight, biomarker levels and quantitative assessment of motor coordination.Treatment of mice with JQ1 induced beneficial effects on some outcome measures, notably a transient increase in weight, reduction of liver cholesterol, and improvements in the footprint test, but these effects occurred only in male but not in female mice. Our results indicate bromodomain proteins as potential therapeutic drug target for NPCD and reveal sex-dependent BET protein signaling in mice.

title: Disrupting SORL1-retromer endosomal recycling in mice drives the age-dependent neurodegenerative signature of Alzheimer's disease
authors: Qureshi, Y. H.; Guo, J.; Rinald, J. H.; Li, Z.; Soni, R. K.; Govindarajan, A.; Tortora, E.; Uzunova, G.; Yang, Y.; Kannan, S.; Nanayakkara, P.; Troy, C. M.; Small, S. A.
abstract: MRI studies have mapped the atrophic signature that distinguishes Alzheimer's disease (AD), isolating regions differentially vulnerable to its age-dependent neurodegenerative process. An endosomal recycling pathway regulated by the interaction of SORL1 with retromer is pathogenically disrupted in AD. Here we test the hypothesis, that the pathway might drive the neurodegenerative process, via multiple yearlong studies in over 140 wildtype and SORL1 deficient mice, modeling SORL1's causative mutations. MRI studies revealed that SORL1 deficiency induced an age-dependent AD-pattern of atrophy, centered on the trans-entorhinal cortex, and that atrophy was prevented by SORL1 restoration, secondary to overexpressing the retromer protein VPS26b. Postmortem studies validated that the atrophy reflects neuronal loss. Proteomic profiling revealed that the atrophy is associated with reductions in cell death suppressors, one of which was then found deficient in the trans-entorhinal cortex of AD patients. Besides supporting the hypothesis, when taken together with other findings the results suggest that SORL1-retromer disruptions represent a therapeutically-amenable common 'neurodegeneration pathway' in AD.

title: Psychedelics restructure information in the human brain
authors: Blackburne, G.; Liardi, A.; Mallaroni, P.; McAlpine, R.; Carhart-Harris, R.; Timmermann, C.; Muthukumaraswamy, S. D.; Skipper, J. I.; Mediano, P. A. M.
abstract: How do psychedelic drugs alter human brain function? Answering this question relies on our ability to understand how information is stored, transferred, and transformed across the cortex. Here, we leverage a precise mathematical framework for multivariate information decomposition to construct the first comprehensive picture of these processes across five compounds: LSD, psilocybin, ketamine, DMT and 5-MeO-DMT (N=80). We provide a formal and empirical explanation of major prior results, revealing sets of competing underlying phenomena masked by extant approaches. We extend this analysis to novel higher-order phenomena, and we demonstrate how all of these observations can emerge from a minimal generative model in which neural populations operate with reduced self-coupling. In sum, our results suggest that the psychedelic brain is one in which cortical populations become alike, but not necessarily together. This has important implications for models of how psychedelics reorganize brain dynamics to alter subjective experience and alleviate mental health conditions.

title: Activity drives local CaMKII synthesis and subcellular localization via autophosphorylation-dependent pathways
authors: Clements, K. J.; Chen, N.; Gonzalez, K. M. D. L.; Zhang, Y.; Rodal, A. A.; Griffith, L.
abstract: Strong repeated stimulation of a neuron triggers an increase in local protein synthesis along with a change in localization of proteins, allowing the neuron to rapidly adjust its proteome in response to activity. One of these proteins, calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), is involved in mediating structural and functional changes after activity. While postsynaptic CaMKII translation has been studied, very little is known about presynaptic synthesis, including its mechanisms and the functional consequences. We utilized the Drosophila larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ) as a model to study the molecular requirements for activity-dependent synthesis along with the localization of CaMKII protein. Presynaptic-specific tagging of endogenous CaMKII demonstrates that spaced stimulation rapidly increases presynaptic CaMKII through local translation of pre-existing mRNA, independently of somatic factors. This activity-dependent synthesis requires the distal 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of the CaMKII mRNA, which is also necessary for steady-state synaptic accumulation. Additionally, we show that activity-dependent synthesis requires CaMKII T287 autophosphorylation-induced activation of the PI3K/Akt/mTor pathway. While activity-dependent redistribution of CaMKII has been previously identified, very little is known about how local synthesis and translocation may interact to define different pools of protein that may have distinct functions. We demonstrate that CaMKII with a T287D phosphomimetic mutant localizes to the synaptic membrane and pulse-chase experiments show that the localization of newly-synthesized CaMKII differs from pre-existing CaMKII, indicating neuronal activity generates spatially distinct, and likely functionally distinct, CaMKII populations which may underlie long-lasting plasticity.
